tweets.author: Serenity
tweets.text:
Now that we're close to 2027 it's a good idea to stress test downside scenarios where you have:

1. Capex cuts past 2028 
2. Stranded Compute / DC Slowdowns 
3. Finance deterioration (base case)
4. 2x+ rate hikes

Working in parallel and see what happens with valuations of AI longs. 

If you see acceleration despite all 4, I'd argue that's an opportunity. 

> Next-gen of photonics is one of the rare segments with an extreme rise in optical content and ASPs that can offset aggregate capex cuts. 

Everyone’s moving into that space, including Elon Musk doing M&A, Marvell, Samsung and others with M&A… and we haven’t seen economic impact on emerging architectures even hit players from Celestial to Ayar + their suppliers yet. 

If we look at a scenario where there's excess GPUs but power constraints:

We might see slowdown in aggregate accelerator/GPU/ASIC procurement, but your optical engines + light sources + switches players see acceleration.

Especially as incentive to replace power inefficient networking... since different (cheap BOM) optical architectures improves GPU utilization or even HBM requirements.  

So value migrates to players more high-beta to architectural shifts. 

If Celestial projections are $500m -> $1B, and we expect -30% aggregate capex cuts, I'd argue we'd still see upward revisions from Celestial over the next 2 years.

But financing with #3 matters a lot as seen with $AAOI dropping off of a $550M, vs. $COHR getting prepayments for capacity expansion from their customers. 

Companies that rely on external foundries might be less sensitive to #3 since they're not as capex intensive. 

On the other hand, companies in sectors have a lot of floating interest like certain Neoclouds, and require further financing might be the most impacted. 

> Legacy and specialty memory is a different cycle that markets conflate with AI capex.

If consumer demand weakens but at the same time, players like Windbond exits DDR2, pricing durability is longer than markets expect. 

> Wafer/substrate procurement such as ABF, SOI, InP are low cost but large downstream destruction if not secured, so we’ll likely see acceleration here as seen with $NVDA earnings call. 

> qualification cycle players within bottlenecks remain very compelling, since first revenue in a large TAM, relative to MC is material to that company. 

If a company is valued at $400m then they get a $200m of orders, it's more asymmetrical to a certain company than a rounding error to a $50B incumbent revenue. 
_

There’s period of times where prices are dislocated from fundamentals from leveraged players getting wiped. I’d argue that time is now. 

I disagree with a lot of the stupid "it's over takes" but I agree it's a good idea to haircut future capex expectations and forward valuations due to financing tightening + macro. 

It's also good idea to see the nuances and stress test downside cases. 

But TLDR: I'd argue next phase of AI infrastructure is going to be increasingly disconnected from aggregate AI capex growth. 

I just personally wrote 4 things I'm using to stress test jointly some of the names I'm looking at, so I'm more comfortable waiting things out... despite seeing hedge funds getting liquidated left and right and overwhelming short positioning. 

I personally see acceleration in more narrow parts of the supply chain, while markets treat the entire AI trade as one.  

We'll see how things play out on longer horizons.

tweets.author: Serenity
tweets.text:
$NVDA earnings transcript + industry read through. To sum it up: "Demand far exceeds supply".  

- Good news for the $MU / Samsung memory longs: 

"Our supply commitments increased from $279B last quarter to $390B, primarily related to the multi-year procurement of memory supply". (from SEC filings, not call)

This is a a major leap Q/Q in supply procurement.  

- "We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year-over-year, up from 70%." (upward revision, likely due to capacity constraints easing)

(new agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics support additional ABF substrate capacity)

- NVIDIA said industry cloud backlog increased from $2 trillion to $2.5 trillion in a single quarter. While GPU rental pricing is continuing to rise dramatically:

Hopper GPUs: 2x their original pricing
B300 GPUs: +60% since introduction
Utilization: NVIDIA says its own compute is fully utilized across the hyperscalers and neoclouds it serves.

- "Our co-packaged optics roadmap remains on track"

Optical networking keeps growing rapidly ($21B+ in quarterly networking), CPO scale out switches has entered volume production. With Lambda earlier announcing production deployment of Nvidia photonics CPO switches. 

- "Under these agreements, we will earn revenue on the upfront sale of our infrastructure" So there's additional recurring economics coming from Neoclouds. 

But just points to industry acceleration from memory to CPO to neoclouds, relative to markets pricing in collapse.

tweets.author: Serenity
tweets.text:
I'll leave it up to your judgement. From my point of view, there's $956M in commitments vs. $605M cash so they needed more financing for their buildout. 

However two things stood out:

1. Management commentary around financing: CFO said US bank financing could reach $500m, and that profits would help fund operations. CFO said share price mattered and that they'd lean more into debt. 

So their actions went contrary to management commentary. 

If you look at $COHR, they fund capacity expansion from upfront prepayments. There's other ways to do it too like convertible notes.

2. Capital allocation issue: they spent $102M on three Texas buildings they had under lease. Which was around $5M annualized and I'm sure they're aware market financing conditions are tight. 

2 weeks after buying buildings when they were already relatively low on cash... AOI decided to do yet another $550M ATM. 

It's just a bit hard to justify.

> Founded $NVDA and pioneered GPU computing
> Took an extraordinary gamble in CUDA, despite the company close to bankruptcy risk. 
> Bet paid off heavily, and Nvidia was there as the infrastructure for deep learning and generative AI.

> Devoted his life to establishing American AI leadership

This feels like a horrible joke. Jensen Huang was the pinnacle of visionary tech CEOs and living the American dream.

Ousting Jensen Huang will go down as one of most consequential and darkest decisions in recent US history.

tweets.author: Serenity
tweets.text:
Just to state the nuances of my opinion: Jensen is irreplaceable to $NVDA.

No other CEO can visit a chicken shop in Korea, noodle shop in Japan

And rally hundred of billions of capital and supply chain commitment into Nvidia’s next technological vision.

As for Nvidia: the their roadmap is intact, their existing commitment and revenues are still preserved under Jensen’s leadership.

They’ll still be around 5-10 years from now, given how fundamentally important they are to AI supply chains. 

Under a new leader they can still continue growing if AI demand is intact and maintain their current lines.

But I don’t know anyone who can possibly think that under anyone else, whether it’s Tim Cook or an accountant:

That Nvidia could compound 70% capacity constrained growth Y/Y, without a leader like Jensen making these transformational bets.

As for AI implications:

I’m heavily bullish directionally, given AI is the most transformational technology in human history.

- I expect some potential slowdown in Nvidia’s ecosystem.

I don’t think an accountant can make the same aggressive level of commitments to Neoclouds or supply chains in Taiwan, Korea, Japan beyond existing architectures.

Then rally the capital and trust to make it happen.

- I do expect the next CEO to be more politically aligned with Washington in restricting China GPU access

- I also see the next CEO being less supportive of open weight models (positive for OpenAI/Anthropic)

- I’m less optimistic on $NVDA maintaining their competitive advantages against $AMD, $AVGO, and hyperscalers.

One person doesn’t break the AI trade, I expect companies from optics to memory to still outperform.

However, my confidence in the next leg of Nvidia’s growth, beyond their current roadmap, has been shaken without Jensen Huang.
